pieces.question: Which level does your state fall into?

pieces.caption: jurisdictions sit in the high group

alt: A choice card asking which of four levels a state falls into, None, Low, Moderate or High, beside a card showing nine jurisdictions in the high group.
caption: The four levels the state table sorts every state into. Laws change, so confirm yours.

pieces.eyebrow: Four columns that earn their place

pieces.text: Hours, color coding, and a paragraph per child per day.

alt: A table of the four record keeping columns, Date, Subject, What part and How it went, with example entries, next to a note on what to leave off.
caption: An example entry for each of the four columns. Copy it into whatever you already open every day.

pieces.text: Include something from October and something from March on the same subject.

alt: A table of what to keep in a portfolio for math, writing, reading and science, with a note to include October and March samples of the same subject.
caption: A rough guide to what to keep per subject. Adjust it to what your state asks for.

pieces.title: Work through these in order
items: Where you are in each curriculum

pieces.text: Write approximate dates as approximate. October to December, not a made up Tuesday.

alt: A checklist of places to rebuild a homeschool year from, such as workbooks, library history and photos, beside a note on approximate dates.
caption: Where to look, in order. Mark reconstructed terms as reconstructed.

pieces.question: What did the check tell you?

pieces.text: Ask weeks later, not at the end of the lesson. Four questions, written down.

alt: A choice card listing the four possible results of a learning check, ending in Not enough to say, beside a note to ask weeks after the lesson.
caption: The four possible results of a short check. Not enough to say is a real answer.

pieces.text: Say what was hard. A portfolio with no difficulties reads as curated.

alt: A printable-style folder list for a homeschool evaluation with six items, from the activity log to a note per subject, and a note about saying it plainly.
caption: The six things to bring. Ask your own evaluator or state what it requires.

pieces.title: If your state counts days
items: A tick, or hours if state counts
One or two words: what was covered

alt: A three-part attendance record checklist of date, tick and a few words, beside a comparison of what counts as a school day and what is pointless to log.
caption: The lightest attendance record, and what is not worth writing down.

alt: A daily entry form with four lines, date, subject and part, how it went and an occasional sentence, next to a choice of easy, about right or difficult.
caption: The three things to record each time, plus the occasional fourth.

pieces.caption: Florida and New Hampshire list a portfolio kept two years

alt: A table sorting homeschool papers into keep, keep permanently, photograph and recycle, with a card noting two states that name a two year portfolio period.
caption: Which papers to keep, photograph or recycle. Check your state before discarding anything.

steps.what: Spare. Leave it empty when you plan.
The full plan, or a lighter one

pieces.text: On a short day we always do: two or three things, no more.

alt: A weekly timeline with full plan days and Wednesday left spare on purpose, plus a fill-in note for what a short day always includes.
caption: One way to lay out the week. Pick the spare day that suits yours.

pieces.text: Plan four and manage four, and you have not failed. The work done is identical.

alt: A table showing how many days a week each subject gets in a four-day plan, with a note that planning four and managing four is the same work as five.
caption: An example spread of subjects across four days. Change the numbers to fit your child.

items: Look up your state education site
Note if it repeats each year
Keep a copy and the filing date

pieces.text: The official source is the one that counts. Laws change.

alt: A five-step checklist for finding a state's homeschool notice of intent, from the education website to keeping a copy, with a note that the official source counts.
caption: Five steps to find what applies to you. Confirm against your state's official source.

pieces.question: Does my state ask for days, hours, both or neither?

pieces.text: Mark a day as you go. A box ticked on the day beats a June reconstruction.

alt: A choice card asking whether a state counts days, hours, both or neither, beside a note to mark each day as you go.
caption: The one question to answer at the start of the year, from the official source.

steps.what: Once, from your state education department
A notice, records, a review, or nothing
Do it early and keep a copy
Date, subject and part, one word on how

pieces.text: The curriculum and the perfect schedule do not have to be settled in week one.

alt: A four-step timeline for the first month of homeschooling, from finding state rules to starting a record, with a note on what can wait.
caption: The first-month order, from the official source to a first dated entry.

pieces.text: Log it once for each child, in a line each, with that child's own note.

alt: A comparison of one shared homeschool file against one record per child, with a note on logging a shared morning once for each child.
caption: Why records are filed by child, and how to log a lesson you did together.

pieces.text: Abandoned books belong on the list. A child who may stop may keep starting.

alt: A three-column reading log layout for book, started and finished or stopped, with a note that abandoned books belong on the list.
caption: The three columns of a reading log. Once they can write, let the child fill it in.

steps.what: Check the step before this one is solid
Only if time, amount and step are right

pieces.text: Change one thing at a time, smallest first.

alt: A four-step timeline for a homeschool subject that is not working, from changing the time to changing the material, with a note to change one thing at a time.
caption: The order to try changes in, cheapest first.
